drills.title: vs xarav973 (841) — Scotch Game
drills.coachNote: White's idea was Qxf7+, trying to drag your king out while his queen and rooks swarm your position. You were up a huge amount, and Qxa3 grabbed a pawn but left the queen on a3 offside, so White answered Qxf5 and then Qxb4, picking up your pawns and pulling ahead in activity. Rc1 and Qf4 kept the pressure on, and you gave back a big chunk of your edge. Qxd1 is the cleaner answer: it wins a whole rook, and if White throws in Qxf7+ Kxf7 Rxd1, you're simply up a queen for nothing. Take the biggest piece first, then check the checks.
drills.threat: White's queen on h5 is eyeing f7, and your queen on d3 is attacking his rook on d1, which is guarded only by your bishop-free back rank.

drills.explanation: Bxf2+ forks the king on g1 and the rook on e1 — one of them falls next move. In the game, Bf6 ran into Ng5, costing about 1.6 pawns of advantage.
drills.title: vs xarav973 (841) — Scotch Game
drills.coachNote: White wanted to consolidate with Ng5, hitting your bishop and letting his queen on h5 and knight join an attack on your kingside. You played Bf6 to cover, but after Ng5 Bxg5 Qxg5 f4 White got his pieces active and cut your lead down. You had a much better move: Bxf2+ pulls the king into the corner with Kh1, then Bf7 kicks the queen and Bxe1 wins the exchange after Qg5. Notice that f2 was loose the whole time. When you're winning, forcing a check that wins material beats a defensive move that just holds things together.
drills.threat: Your bishop on h4 and queen on c2 both bear on f2, where White's king is guarded by little more than his rook and queen.

drills.title: vs AlfredoPig (770) — Four Knights Game Double Spanish Variation
drills.coachNote: White wanted Nf5 with Rd7 next, invading your position along the d-file and leaving your king facing threats on g7. Your Qb6 retreated the queen but gave up the centre, so Nf5 came with tempo, then Rd7, Qc3 and Qg6 left you scrambling on the back rank. The position was level, and you turned it into a nearly four-pawn deficit. Qe3 is the answer: it hits d3 and g3 at once, so after Qxc7 Qxd3+ Ka1 Rd7 your queen is active and traps his pieces instead of hiding. Look for the reply that attacks something before you settle for the retreat.
drills.threat: White's queen on a5 attacks your queen on c5 and the c7 pawn, and his knight on g3 is ready to hop to f5.

drills.title: vs AlfredoPig (770) — Four Knights Game Double Spanish Variation
drills.coachNote: White wanted Ng3, reinforcing e4 and f5 while planning Qe6-type ideas against your queen. Your a5 was a slow pawn push, and after Ng3 Qe6 Qe2 a4 White solved his problems with a comfortable position. You gave away a real edge. The move was cxd3: it opens lines against White's king, and after Ng3 dxc2+ Qxc2 Rxd1+ Rxd1 you've traded into a position where you're ahead a pawn. Grab the free pawn when it also forces White to react to your ideas, rather than making a quiet move.
drills.threat: White's knight is about to jump from e2 to g3, and his pawn on d3 is hanging to your pawn on c4.

drills.explanation: Rc7 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Qb3 ran into Bxd3, costing about 4.3 pawns of advantage.
drills.title: vs Wuranti (790) — London System
drills.coachNote: Black wanted to trade off the attackers with Bxd3, and it hit the mark since your queen on b3 left the c-file and the knight on b5 loose. After Bxd3 Nxa7 Kxa7 Qxb4 you got a mess and Black came out ahead by a lot. You had a fine equal position and threw away over four pawns. Rc7 was the fix: after Qxc7 Nxc7 Bxd3 Re1 Kxc7 the tactics balance out and your pieces stay safe. Before you make a quiet move, check what your knight on b5 needs to stay protected.
drills.threat: Black's bishop on d3 is attacking your rook on c1... no, it's capturing your bishop, and your knight on b5 is under fire from his bishop on g6 and queen on d7.

drills.title: vs Wuranti (790) — London System
drills.coachNote: Black wanted to trade the bishops with Bxh2+, which drags your king to h2 and lets his pieces gain tempo. You moved your bishop to h2 and Black played Bxh2+ Kxh2 Kb8 Ne5, and your big edge evaporated because your king got exposed. You were winning and gave back over three pawns. Nb5 was better: after Bxf4 Nxa7+ Kc7 exf4 Bxd3 you've won a pawn with a safe king. When you're winning, put the piece where it attacks something instead of the square where it can be traded off.
drills.threat: Black's bishop on d6 is defended only by the pawn and rook, and your knight can jump to b5 to hit it and a7.

drills.coachNote: Black wanted to trade knights with Nxe5 and follow with Qc7, hitting your bishop on f4 and your pawn on e5. Your b4 pushed a pawn but loosened c3, so after Nxe5 dxe5 Qc7 Be2 you were on the back foot. You were clearly better and it slipped away. Nf3 was the answer: it keeps the knight safe and after Nb6 a4 Nc4 Bxc4 dxc4 you keep your structure and the advantage. Retreat the knight before you push a pawn that weakens your position.
drills.threat: Black's knight on d7 can capture your knight on e5, and your pawn on c3 is the only thing holding your queenside together.

drills.coachNote: Black wanted to trade off your bishop with Bxe5 and put a queen on c7, hitting your pawn structure. You played Qe1, which didn't deal with that, so Bxe5 dxe5 Qc7 f4 left you with weak pawns on e5 and c3. You lost a good chunk of your edge. Bf4 was the better move: it keeps the bishop on the diagonal, and after Rxc3 Qd2 Rc8 Rfc1 Bf6 your pieces get active. Deal with the piece that's under fire before you improve your queen.
drills.threat: Black's rook on c8 eyes your pawn on c3, and his bishop on g7 is lined up against your bishop on e5.

drills.title: vs fantagalo (819) — Ruy Lopez Opening
drills.coachNote: White's pawns on c5, d6 and e6 have your king and knight boxed in, and his rook on b6 is waiting to land on b8 with check. You were already worse here, but Kd8 stepped straight onto that back rank. Rb8+ forced your knight to c8, then c6 and Rh7 followed, and the position went from a fight to roughly -10. Kc8 answers by staying off the back-rank checks. After c6 Bc4 dxe7 Kc7, your king walks back toward the pawns and Rb7+ is only a check, not a mating net. When you're in check, pick the square that leaves the enemy rook no forcing entry.
drills.threat: White's pawn on d6 is checking your king on c7, and his Rb6 is one step from a back-rank check on b8.

drills.title: vs fantagalo (819) — Ruy Lopez Opening
drills.coachNote: Your c5 pawn was attacked by the b4 pawn and the Rc1. Meanwhile his d5 pawn, cramping your knight on e7, had no real defender, and your knight on e7 attacks it. Kd7 ignored all that and put your king on the d-file, so after Rxc5 Rc8 White got e6+ with tempo and Kd8 was forced. You dropped a pawn and the initiative, and the eval went from level to about -3. Nxd5 takes the loose pawn and hits his Rb6 at the same time. After Rxc5+ Rc7 Rbc6 Rxc6 Nxc6, the rooks come off and you're fine. When a pawn is hanging and your piece can take it, check that capture before any king move.
drills.threat: White's d5 pawn is loose, and his Rc1 and b4 pawn are both bearing down on your c5 pawn.

drills.title: vs 1asaka (728) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: White's king has no air. Your Rf2 already covers f1 and h2, your queen on c6 looks down the long diagonal, and g2 is the hole in his position. That meant Qg2 was checkmate, since the rook on f2 protects the queen and his own Rh1 blocks the king's escape. Rxb2 grabbed a pawn, but it pulled your rook off f2, which was the mating piece. Nd2 then covered things, Qc2 and Rh2 followed, and you had to work to win a position that was already over. Qg2# ends it on the spot, and Rg2+ or Rdf8 would also have kept the mate. When the enemy king is boxed in, count checks before you count pawns.
drills.threat: White's king on g1 is boxed in by his own rook on h1, and your queen's diagonal to g2 is open.

drills.title: vs 1asaka (728) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: White's pieces were tangled: the Nb1, Ra1 and Rh1 were all doing nothing, and your bishop on e5 was the piece stopping them from waking up. A quiet a6 gave him the free move he needed. Re1 came with tempo, Rde8 was forced-ish, and then b3 and h5 let White untangle. You were up nearly 5 pawns and this cost about 1.7 of it. Qf3 puts your queen on the diagonal to his Rh1, so the rook has to move. After Rd1 Rde8 Re1 Bd6 a4 your pieces stay active while his are still passive. When you're ahead, use each move to keep his worst pieces trapped.
drills.threat: White wants Re1 next, hitting your bishop on e5 with tempo and unlocking his stuck knight and rooks.

drills.title: vs Bramthechessguy (842) — Indian Game East Indian London System
drills.coachNote: Black's rook on e2 and bishop on f5 are lined up on c2 and b1, right next to your king on c1. You were already down a lot, but Qxc4 took the knight and dragged your queen onto the c-file. Rc2+ Kb1 was forced, and then Rxc3+ was a discovered check from the Bf5 while the rook hit your queen on c4. You lost the queen for nothing, and it cost about 4 pawns of eval. Qb3 keeps your queen guarding b2 and away from the c-file. After Rxb2 Qxb2 Nxb2 Kxb2 you trade your queen for a rook and knight, which is the best you can get here. Before you capture, check what the enemy rook and bishop attack once your piece moves.
drills.threat: Your Qa4 and Nf3 look busy, but Black's Re2 and Bf5 are aiming at your c2 square and king.

drills.title: vs Bramthechessguy (842) — Indian Game East Indian London System
drills.coachNote: Look at the e-file: Black's Re8 is pinned onto your Be2, with your king on e1 behind it, and only that king defends the bishop. Black wanted Bd3 to attack the pinned bishop, and dxc5 grabbed a pawn without dealing with it. After Bd3 you had to defend with Ng1, Black recaptured with dxc5, and then O-O-O gave him a big lead. You were slightly worse before, but this made it much worse. Kf1 breaks the pin on the spot, so Bd3 has no target. After a6 Qd1 Qb6 Nb3 Nc6, your position holds together. When a piece is pinned to your king, fix the pin first.
drills.threat: Black's rook on e8 pins your Be2 to the king on e1, and his Bf5 wants to hit it.

drills.coachNote: That Nf5 was White's best piece. It attacks d6, h6 and g7, and it was backed by e4, so he could build up on your king. b6 was a slow move that left it there, and after Ng3 Nd4 b3 White regrouped and got to play Ng4 against your pieces. You had a small edge and gave some of it back. Bxf5 exf5 trades your bishop for that monster, and it turns his pawn structure into a target. Then Qd7 hits f5 and Nd4 gets a strong central knight, and you're comfortable. When the enemy has a knight you don't like, trade it before it does damage.
drills.threat: White's knight on f5 is a strong outpost, eyeing d6, h6 and g7 near your king, and it's protected by the e4 pawn.

drills.title: vs Abfab18 (791) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: You're up a bishop for nothing here, so the job is simple: keep it clean. Your Bc4 hits e6, and Black's king wants Kf7 to guard that pawn and free itself. Kf4 is also playable, but the engine likes Kf3 better, and in the game Black got Kf7, e4 Ke7 Ke3. So don't panic about the swing, it's still winning. Kf3 heads to e3 and lets you play e4, locking Black's pawns while your king stays behind them. From there Kf7 e4 Ke7 Ke3 Kf7 shows how easy the plan is. In won endgames, walk your king toward the pawn break you're going to play.
drills.threat: Black's king wants to reach f7 to protect e6, and your bishop on c4 is keeping it out.

drills.explanation: Ba2 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Bb3 ran into Ke7, costing about 9.8 pawns of advantage.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs Abfab18 (791) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: The whole plan in this endgame is to march your king to c4 and b5 and win Black's queenside pawns. Bb3 clears c4 but wastes time: Black plays Ke7, you play Kc4, Black gets Kf7, and now the bishop on b3 is stuck behind your king and has to spend a move on Ba2 anyway. You were up nearly 20 pawns, so the win was never at risk, but you gave Black free tempi. Ba2 clears c4 in one move, keeps the a2-g8 diagonal aimed at Black's e6 pawn, and lets the king go Kc4, Kb5 while Black shuffles Ke7, Ke8, Kd8. When a piece is in your king's way, move it once, to the square where it will end up.
drills.threat: Your king wants c4 and then b5 to pick off Black's queenside pawns, but your own bishop is standing on c4.

drills.title: vs osmanahma (728) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Black wanted Qxd2, and it's mate: the queen lands on d2 next to your king on e1, and the rook on f2 protects it. You were up 5.6 pawns, yet Rf1 only attacked the rook and ignored that the d2 knight was pinned in place by two attackers against one defender. Qxd2# ended the game on the spot. Qd7+ is the answer because it's a check with tempo: Black's king must go to f6, and then O-O-O puts your rook on d1 to guard d2 and takes your king off the e1 square. From there you're still winning. Before you grab a tempo, count the attackers on your loose pieces.
drills.threat: Black's queen on g5 and rook on f2 both hit your knight on d2, which only your king guards.

drills.explanation: Qg6+ forks the king on e8 and the rook on h5 — one of them falls next move. In the game, Qd4 ran into Qd7, costing about 5.2 pawns of advantage.

drills.title: vs osmanahma (728) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Black wanted a quiet move to get his queen out and his king safe, and Qd4 gave him that time. His rook on h5 was hanging to a check: Qg6+ can't be blocked and the king has to step aside. After Qd4 he played Qd7, then Bf4 and Qh7, and later ...Qa4+ gave him real counterplay when you were 6 pawns up. Qg6+ forces Kd7, and then Qxh5 wins the rook for free. Nd4+ follows, and Black's king is stuck in the open. When a check picks up loose material, play it before he can tidy his pieces.
drills.threat: Black's rook on h5 is undefended, and your queen on d3 sees g6 with check.

drills.title: vs debaser7 (798) — Slav Defense
drills.coachNote: White wanted to push b6-b7 and promote, and the only thing stopping that was your rook on the c-file. Rc4+ was a check that looked active, but it let White's king step to d5 with a tempo on your rook, and that was the end of your defence. After Rc3 b7 Rb3 the pawn queens, and you had no way to stop it. You were already losing at -7.4, and Rc1 was the most stubborn try. It goes back to c1 so that after b7, Re1+ gives a check with tempo, and then Rb1 holds the b-file from behind.
drills.threat: White's b-pawn is one step from b7, and his king on e4 wants d5 to kick your rook off the c-file.

drills.title: vs debaser7 (798) — Slav Defense
drills.coachNote: White's two connected pawns on a6 and b5 can only be stopped by a rook that stays in front of them or behind them. Rc7 put your rook on the one square where b6 attacks it with tempo. After b6 you had to run to c1, b7 followed, and Ra1 was too slow. Losing was likely at -6.5, but you made it easy. Ra7 attacks the a6 pawn directly and keeps the rook on the seventh where it blockades. Then Re8, Kh5 and Kd6 get your king toward the queenside while your rook keeps checking from the side, and you have real defensive chances. A rook in front of passed pawns must stay off squares that pawn moves attack.
drills.threat: White's b5 pawn wants b6, hitting your rook on the seventh and clearing the way for a6-a7.

drills.title: vs Himanshu_Nagar04 (882) — London System
drills.coachNote: White's rook on b7 and king on the queenside had Black's king boxed in on e8. Black's only free piece was the bishop on f5, and he wanted to use it to give the king breathing room. Kc6 let him play Bg4, then Kd6 forced Kf8 and Black's king escaped the net before Re7 could seal it. That threw away a position with eval +67, a forced win. Kb4 is a quieter move that keeps the net intact. After Bh3, Kc5 pushes Black's king back with Kd8, Kd6 and Kc8, so his king stays boxed on the back rank. A king should come closer to the enemy king without giving it a path out.
drills.threat: Black's king is boxed on e8, so his bishop wants g4 or h3 to free the king toward f8.

drills.explanation: Rb2 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Kb5 ran into Bh3, costing about 49.5 pawns of advantage.
drills.title: vs Himanshu_Nagar04 (882) — London System
drills.coachNote: Black's king on c7 was hitting your rook on b6. You defended it with Kb5, which left your king out in front of your own pawns. Black just waited with Bh3, and after Kc5 Bg4 you had to retreat Rb2 anyway. So you spent two king moves and got the same retreat, having drifted your king out and dropped almost all of your +58 advantage. Rb2 solves it in one move: the rook is safe from the king and goes off toward the h-file. In the line Bh3, Ka3, Bg4, Rh2 the rook is aimed at g6, while your king stays back to hold the queenside. When a piece is attacked, retreat it before you defend it with a piece you need elsewhere.
drills.threat: Your rook on b6 is attacked by Black's king on c7, and only your king on a4 defends it.

drills.title: vs dexxter92 (816) — Bishops Opening Berlin Vienna Hybrid Variation
drills.coachNote: White's queen on h6 was hitting the f8 rook, and only your rook on f7 kept it defended. You were up 6.6 pawns, but Rh7 moved that defender off f7 to attack the queen, which left the f8 rook hanging with your own rook blocking the h-file. Qxf8# was mate. Qh7 is the fix: it uses your queen to challenge White's on the diagonal from d3 to h7, and after Qxh7+ Kxh7 Bf4 the queens are gone. Then you play Re8 and trade rooks on e8 with your extra material. Before you move a defender, ask what it was guarding.
drills.threat: White's queen on h6 and bishop on e5 are lined up on your f8 rook, guarded only by the rook on f7.

drills.title: vs dexxter92 (816) — Bishops Opening Berlin Vienna Hybrid Variation
drills.coachNote: White's bishop on f6, backed only by the queen on h6, was squeezing you: your rook on h7 was pinned on the h-file and g7 was under fire, so your king had nowhere to go. Kg8 looked like breathing room, but it walked into Qg5+. Your queen had to block on g6, and Qxg6+ simply won it, which turned a hard position into a lost one. Look at what holds White's attack together: the bishop on f6 is defended by just the queen. Rxf6 removes it, and after Qxf6+ Rg7 you block the check, and the bishop on c6 is hanging to Qxc6 but you keep your queen active with Qg6 ideas. When someone is attacking your king, hit the attacker first.

drills.coachNote: Your Qe6 forks both rooks, and Black's only guard on each is the king on f8. Qxg8+ took the wrong one. Kxg8 Rxe8+ Kf7 then hits your rook, so after Re3 you'd swapped your queen for one rook, from +4.6 to a losing position. Qxe8+ is the capture that works: your Re1 stands behind e8, so the king can't recapture, and after ...Kg7 Qd7+ Kh8 Re8 you keep the queen and attack the other rook. Between two captures, check which one your other pieces support, so the capturing piece can't be taken.

drills.coachNote: White's Ng5 was trying to jump into your kingside, but nothing protects it, and your h6 pawn attacks it. Qf5 also hit the knight, but it gave White a tempo to step away. After ...Ne4 Qg6 f3 Raa8, the knight sat on e4 defended by f3, and you had spent time for a free piece that had slipped away. hxg5 simply captures it, and after h3 Qf5 a3 f6 f3 you're a piece up, with your queen coming to f5 anyway. When a piece hangs to a pawn, take it before you ask your queen for more.

drills.coachNote: White's pawn on e6 is the only thing bothering you. It covers f7 and d7, and Qe2 and Re1 are lined up behind it. You were clearly better, about three pawns up. But Bxe6 puts your bishop on a square where Qxe6+ takes it with check along the e6–g8 diagonal. Queens come off after Qxe6 Rxe6, and you've given a bishop for a pawn. Re8 is the calmer move. Your rook hits the pawn a second time, and if Qd1 then Rxe6 Rxe6 Qxe6 wins it cleanly. Count attackers and defenders on e6 before you capture.

drills.title: vs Chess2025king (503) — Englund Gambit
drills.coachNote: Black's idea is simple. The queen on g5 attacks g2, and behind that pawn sits your rook on h1. The position was roughly equal. Your f3 pushes a pawn, but it doesn't guard g2, and it lets the queen take with tempo. After Qxg2 you can't save both rook and structure. Qd2 Qxh1 wins the rook, and Qf2 doesn't get it back. Bf1 answers the threat at once, because the bishop covers g2. Then d5 c4 dxc4 Nc3 develops with a healthy position. When a queen attacks a pawn that has a rook behind it, defend that pawn first.
drills.threat: Black's queen on g5 hits your pawn on g2, and nothing defends it, with your rook on h1 sitting right behind.

drills.title: vs Chess2025king (503) — Englund Gambit
drills.coachNote: Black's pawn on a3 and bishop on a2 are working together against your king on c1. The pawn attacks b2, and the bishop takes away b1 and b3. You were already down a lot, about six pawns, but Rf1 made things much worse. It walks the rook onto a diagonal, and Bc4 hits it. After Rf4, the a-pawn is free to run to a2, and Bc3 piles on. b3 is the move that fights back. It stops the bishop's route to c4 and keeps the pawn on b2 protected. Nc3 then targets the bishop, and Bxb3 cxb3 Bxh4 is much more resilient. Before you move a piece, check which of your squares his bishop and pawn are already controlling.
drills.threat: Black's pawn on a3 attacks your b2 pawn, and his bishop on a2 seals the b1 and b3 squares around your king.

drills.coachNote: Black had two pieces bearing down on c5, the knight on a6 and the bishop on f8. You were better by about a pawn and a half, but Nc5 lands right in that crossfire. Nxc5 dxc5 Bxc5 wins a pawn and leaves the bishop active, and the a4 that follows doesn't repair it. Na5 does something different. It hits b7 and c6 and stays out of the trade. After Qc8 e4 dxe4 Qxe4 Qd7, you're the one with the initiative. Before a knight lands next to enemy pieces, count what already attacks that square.
drills.threat: Black's knight on a6 and bishop on f8 both aim at c5, so any piece landing there gets traded off.

drills.title: vs rubika_ansari (477) — London System...4.c3 Bf5
drills.coachNote: Your queen on h7 already sits in Black's territory. The g8 rook and the queen on d8 can cut off the way home. You were level, and Qxh6 grabs a pawn but goes even deeper. Rg6 attacks the queen, Qh7 goes back, Qf8 closes in, and Nh2 leaves you scrambling. You went from equal to clearly worse. Bg7 is the quieter answer. It puts a bishop on g7 covering f8 and h6, so the queen isn't easily trapped. Nbd7 c4 Ne4 Rad1 Rc8 is a normal game where nothing hangs. A pawn grab isn't worth it when your queen has to walk home through enemy pieces.
drills.threat: Your queen on h7 has wandered deep, and Black's rook on g8 and queen on d8 are ready to cut off its retreat.

drills.coachNote: White's queen on f3 attacks your knight on h5, and nothing defends it. Meanwhile Bb3 is pointed through d5 at your king on g8, with only the f7 pawn in the way. Take the trade that also fixes your loose piece and your king's diagonal.

drills.coachNote: White's Ng6 attacks your rook on f8. But your knight on h5 is still attacked by Qf3 and nothing defends it. You were better by more than a pawn and a half. drills.coachNote: Black's last two pawn moves opened the h5–e8 diagonal, and his king on e8 has lost its f7 cover. You had a forced win on the board, and Bg3 throws it away. You were saving the bishop from g5, which is understandable, but it lets Black play Nh6. Then Qh5+ Nf7 blocks the check and h4 is no longer mate. Qh5# ends the game immediately. The queen goes to h5 with check, and nothing can interpose on g6 or f7, so the game is over. Before you move a piece away from a threat, look for a check that ends the game.
drills.threat: Black's f6 and g5 pushes left the e8 king without an f7 pawn and opened the diagonal from h5.

drills.title: vs EriRenaldo (466) — Queens Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: Black's king has wandered into the open on d3, and his only defenders are the knight on e3 and the rook on f4. Your job was to keep him in the open with checks, and you were completely winning, about +20. Rg3 attacked the knight instead of checking, which gave his king time to step away with Kc4. After Rxe3 Kb5 Rxe5 you still come out ahead, but you let a forced win shrink to a much smaller edge. Rd1+ makes the king decide immediately, and after Ke4 Qh7+ hits the rook on f5 with check. Rde1 and c4 follow, and he never gets a free move. When his king is exposed, keep checking and make him answer.
drills.threat: Black's king on d3 and knight on e3 are far from any cover, and your rooks on g1 and h1 can check him right now.

drills.title: vs VitorSpada23 (560) — Caro Kann Defense
drills.coachNote: The c7-h2 diagonal is completely open: d6, e5, f4 and g3 are all empty. White's h2 pawn is guarded only by the king, and your rook on h8 stands behind it on the h-file. That means Qxh2 is not just a capture, it is mate, because the king can't recapture and f1 is taken by his own rook. Instead you played f5, and White answered g3, which plugs the diagonal. The mate is gone, Nf6 and Ne2 followed, and you ended up losing a game you were winning by a mile. Before any quiet move, look at where your queen is aimed and what protects the target.
drills.threat: White's king on g1 has only the h2 pawn beside it, and your queen on c7 looks straight down the diagonal at it.

The h2 pawn is guarded only by the king on g1, so it is mate on the spot. Taking on f6 gave White a tempo, and he used it for g3, closing the diagonal. After fxg5, a4 and Ne7 the mating idea was gone and so was your advantage. When a forcing win is on the board, play it first and take the pawn later. Qxh2 ends the game right there.
drills.threat: White's pawn on f6 looks like it's asking to be captured, but the real target is the h2 pawn beside his king.

drills.coachNote: Black's king on b8 has almost no room, because your b6 pawn covers a7 and c7. His rooks on e8 and e6 are doing nothing about it. You were already winning, and Rc1 was a slow move that gave him time to counter. He played R6e7, hitting your queen, and after Qg6 Rd8 Qc6 you had to defend instead of attack. Qc7+ was the way to go. The king has to go to a8, because Rc8 and Ka8 lose to the same idea, and then Qa7 is mate with the pawn on b6 covering. When the king has no air, look for the checks before you improve your rook.
drills.threat: Black's king on b8 is boxed in behind your b6 pawn, and your queen on h7 is one check from the queenside.

Qg7 keeps everything tense. It attacks the rook on f8 and after Ka8, Bd5+ Rxd5 Qxf8+ wins a whole rook with check. When you're far ahead, use the pieces that are already aimed at the king before spending time on pawns.
drills.threat: Black's rooks on d8 and f8 protect each other, but your queen on h6 can reach g7 and hit the f8 rook.

Castling short puts your king right in the path of that pawn storm. After O-O, g5 Ne8 gxh6 g6 leaves you cramped, with a weakened king and the h-file opening up, and that cost you about 2.7 pawns. Nfd7 moves the knight before g5 can hit it. Then Nb3 a5 Nd2 e5 gives you central counterplay, and your king stays in the middle instead of walking into the attack. Don't castle toward a pawn storm.

Taking on g5 opened the h-file for his rook straight at your castled king. hxg5 followed, and after e5 gxf6 g6 you lost the knight and the game slid away. Ne8 steps aside and keeps the file closed. After gxh6 g6 h5 e5 dxe5 you still have your king covered. Don't open the file towards your own king.
